part: PART I, LONDON AND THE LAST DIPLOMATIC ATTEMPTS
title: 17 July 1974, The London meeting
body:
Ecevit met with Prime Minister Harold Wilson and Foreign Secretary James Callaghan in London. Turkey was hoping for British involvement in a joint intervention or permission for the Turkish military to use British bases. This meeting would help establish whether Ankara could rely on British cooperation.

In a long speech, Ecevit stated that if Sampson became entrenched, no organization or nation would be able to change the situation in Cyprus, which Turkey could not accept.

Wilson was very attentive. Ecevit stressed that Turkey could not sit back and made his intentions known:

Ecevit: "If you do not want bloodshed and an irreparable wound in NATO, let us conduct the operation together. Agree to allow Turkish forces to use the British bases. If we enter the island from your bases, it will be bloodless. I am calling on you to fulfill your duty under the Treaty of Guarantee."

Wilson responded that the British knew who Sampson was and shared Turkey's concerns:

Wilson: "The opportunity to restore the old order has not yet been lost."

Ecevit: "Every passing hour makes matters a little more difficult. Sampson must be removed and a new order established in Cyprus. The balance has been completely upset. We are determined to secure the Turkish community's safety. For that, the Turks must be given an outlet to the sea..."

Wilson: "Let us invite Greece too and hold a tripartite meeting here. Kissinger is continuing his efforts as well. The United Nations is meeting. There is no need for military action."

Ecevit: "The balance in Cyprus has been upset beyond restoration. This cannot be put right by platonic statements or resolutions. Greece is responsible for the coup and cannot be accepted as a party."

The talks continued, and Wilson tried to push for negotiations:

Wilson: "We are in contact with Greece. We have asked for the replacement of the officers responsible for the coup and are awaiting a reply."

Ecevit remained reasonable and avoided threats. One diplomat at the meeting commented that Ecevit did not make any statements like "if you do not do this, I shall go" as he had done previously.

Ecevit: "We must think humanely. The present Sampson regime will change. If Turkey is forced to act, it will have to do so alone. Blood will be shed, whereas we could settle this by creating as little conflict as possible. The only way to do that is to use your bases."

However, this time it was Callaghan who spoke:

Callaghan: "There will be war with Greece. Athens cannot stand by and watch. NATO will be shaken."

The British prime minister concluded the talks after they had exhausted all possible options:

Wilson: "The status of the bases has been defined quite clearly... There is no possibility of sending Turkish troops out from them... Nor do we accept the view that the Treaty of Guarantee gives Britain the right to armed intervention."

part: PART I, LONDON AND THE LAST DIPLOMATIC ATTEMPTS
title: 18 July 1974, Meeting Sisco
body:
After the talks with the British, Ecevit met with American diplomat Joseph Sisco. Sisco tried to persuade the Turkish delegation not to intervene, but the government needed to make its demands known.

Having heard Ecevit’s demands, Sisco argued forcefully against Turkish intervention. He also brought a message from Kissinger:

Sisco: "America opposes a Turkish intervention because of the coup. We think this could lead to war between two NATO members."

Ecevit said that Turkey did not plan to go to war with Greece. He tried to reassure the American administration by emphasizing the strength of Turkish-American relations. He also said that friendships could last if they were strong and based on equality, and that the Sixth Fleet could now visit Turkish ports more safely.

Ecevit: "...But it is impossible for Turkey to turn a blind eye to a fait accompli in Cyprus."

Sisco: "But you are not considering Greece's reaction. They will not leave this unanswered. War will break out and the region will be thrown into turmoil. You should know that your relations with the United States will also deteriorate."

Ecevit: "That is for them to decide."

The meeting continued over lunch. Sisco, one of Kissinger's closest allies, spoke with Callaghan. When he returned, he still opposed Turkish intervention, but appeared to realize how determined Turkey was to proceed.

Witnesses reported:

Sisco: "Mr. Ecevit, I am going from here to Athens. Give me your conditions in writing. We shall take them to the Greeks. I shall then return to Ankara and inform you of their answers."

Ecevit then dictated his terms:

Ecevit: "Our conditions are quite clear. To restore the balance and secure the Turkish community's safety, the presence of Turkish troops on the island must be accepted. Sampson must be replaced immediately, the Greek officers withdrawn, the Turkish community granted an area with an outlet to the sea, and a system established to control entry to and exit from the island. In other words, Turkey must be granted the opportunities the Greeks currently possess."

Meanwhile, in Ankara, Finance Minister Deniz Baykal gave a speech described by many as "clear and resolute". He explained how the Ecevit government would deal with the crisis and made it clear that it was moving toward intervention.

Baykal: "How does the government view events? In our view, the London and Zurich agreements had lost their validity even before the coup. They continued in practice. The Treaty of Guarantee was also losing its effectiveness, and Turkey was unable to protect its rights arising from the agreements. This is the underlying cause of the latest events. We must now do more than explain our rights; we must take matters further. We shall seek our rights on the basis of an independent Cyprus. Our first objective is to ensure that the Turkish community obtains at least one port. There is a movement in the world to bring Makarios back. But that is not our objective. If we act, paths beyond London and Zurich may open before us. We do not regard the latest developments as a simple coup..."

part: PART I, LONDON AND THE LAST DIPLOMATIC ATTEMPTS
title: 19 July 1974, The Greek response
body:
Sisco left with the conditions set by Ecevit, but it remained unclear whether the Greeks would agree to the changes needed to avoid Turkish intervention. The answer had to come from the Greek leadership, and time was running out for a diplomatic resolution.

The meeting between Sisco and Ioannidis had been very tense.

"Ioannidis absolutely did not believe in a Turkish intervention. Despite all Sisco's efforts, he did not change his attitude. When he read the conditions sent by Ecevit, he became angry and said, 'They might as well have asked for Athens too; if they are so confident, let them make a landing.' He said that in such a case war would certainly break out and Greece would attack Turkey. These words probably had to be taken seriously. Ioannidis continually spoke of Makarios's immorality and his cooperation with the Russians. He said that Sampson's arrival had settled the Cyprus problem at its root. He was in a strange state of mind. He did not want to listen to anyone and told Sisco to stop the Turks, otherwise NATO would collapse."

The Greek leadership was reluctant to accept the Turkish proposals. U.S. Ambassador to Greece Henry Tasca had advised Kissinger that the Sixth Fleet should be stationed between Cyprus and Turkey to prevent an intervention. Kissinger replied:

Kissinger: "NO. Do not become hysterical."

"The main worry was that it could involve the Soviets. It would be another—a second Johnson letter—and we would lose Turkey entirely," Sisco continued.

Sisco: "I have spoken with the Greek authorities. There are important changes in their position. In particular, they agree to replace the officers involved in the coup. Moreover, after a certain transitional period, it appears possible that Sampson could be replaced by someone more moderate. They promise elections and have stated in particular that no harm will come to the Turks' safety. Sampson has also made statements to this effect. They guarantee that intercommunal talks will begin immediately."

A cold silence filled the room. Athens had refused to meet any of the vital Turkish demands. These included joint administration of key seaports and airports, acceptance of Turkish troops with facilities equal to those enjoyed by the Greeks, and an immediate change of government. They had also refused to give the Turkish community access to the sea.

They were giving reassurances but no real guarantees.

part: PART II, THE FIRST OPERATION AND GENEVA I: CONTINUED OPERATIONS
title: 27–28 July 1974: Fighting on the Flanks
body:
Our initial refusal to freeze the frontlines had resulted in the ceasefire being increasingly theoretical in nature. While the Geneva negotiations continued to progress slowly without significant agreement, our forces continued to attempt to remove hostile positions in the periphery of the Turkish-held enclave and establish a more defensible perimeter before any political settlement would have the ability to permanently freeze the situation on the ground.

At the meeting of experts in Geneva which continued until seven in the morning of 28 July, neither side was able to make significant progress on its existing position. The Greeks demanded that the UN peacekeeping force be placed inside a very narrow security zone and insisted upon the withdrawal, supply restrictions and non-increase of foreign troops on the island. They demanded the return of refugees to their homes and continued to reject our calls to create a broader territorial arrangement for the Turkish Cypriot community. The Turkish delegation, meanwhile, remained unwilling to accept a settlement that would return the island to a similar insecure state that had been in place prior to our intervention.

While the diplomats engaged in arguments, fighting continued to break out around the periphery of our positions. The villages of Karavas, Lapithos and Myrtou remained in the hands of the National Guard while Turkish forces had succeeded in capturing Buffavento Castle. These positions were becoming increasingly integral to the security of our western and mountain approaches, but taking them would represent yet another expansion of our territorial holdings at a time when we were already being accused of ignoring the ceasefire.

The military situation thus once again placed us in the same position. We could continue to clear hostile positions in our periphery, strengthen our western approaches and take strategically valuable ground prior to Geneva succeeding in freezing the frontlines. Such actions would improve our military position but could further damage the conference while reinforcing Greek assertions that Turkey had no intention of respecting the ceasefire. Alternatively, we could finally halt our forces at their existing positions and place our remaining demands solely in the hands of our delegation at Geneva.

part: PART II, THE FIRST OPERATION AND GENEVA I: CONTINUED OPERATIONS
title: 29–30 July 1974: Geneva I Concludes
body:
The First Geneva Conference had now entered its final days, but despite days of negotiations, little meaningful progress had been achieved. Our forces had continued to expand and consolidate their positions throughout the conference, using the ineffective ceasefire to their advantage whenever enemy fire or exposed positions provided a justification for further movement. For the Greek delegation and increasingly for the British, these actions had become proof that Turkey was negotiating in Geneva while simultaneously changing the reality on the ground.

The airport question had only worsened the situation. British Foreign Minister Callaghan had blown the matter increasingly out of proportion, treating the status of Nicosia Airport almost as a question of British prestige and repeatedly allowing it to dominate negotiations far beyond its real importance. With Turkish forces having already accepted that the airport itself would not be taken, the continuing British insistence on the matter became yet another source of unnecessary tension in a conference already struggling to bring a deal to fruition.

At the conference, the airport question was once more being discussed, and the British delegation insisted that its formula be accepted. Eventually, Turan Güneş spoke up:

“This conference must end. Mr. Callaghan, let us leave the airport question to the technicians and take it up at the second conference... If you accept this, I would like to speak privately with Mr. Mavros.”

Despite all of these disputes, Geneva had not been totally without result. By the end of the conference, something that had failed to exist since the ceasefire of 22 July had finally been achieved on the island: an actual halt to the movement of the frontlines. Both Turkish and Greek forces were increasingly holding their positions rather than trying to further extend them, and the ceasefire was finally taking shape, in practice rather than merely on paper.

For the Turkish Cypriot population, this was of immense importance. The threat posed by the roaming Greek Cypriot militias and continued attacks had not disappeared, but with the fronts finally stabilizing and international attention now firmly focussed on enforcing the ceasefire, the danger facing the isolated Turkish communities had become significantly less than it had only days previously.

Yet our actions throughout the conference had come with a cost. Britain had become increasingly hostile towards our continued advances, Greece accused us of using Geneva simply to legitimize territorial expansion, and even the United States had become increasingly concerned by the constant advances of Turkish forces despite repeated ceasefire demands. Militarily, though, our position was now incomparably stronger than it had been when the operation had begun.

Atilla I had achieved what it could achieve.

Our forces had landed successfully, established the junction between the coastal and airborne formations, taken Kyrenia, secured a continuous Turkish-held corridor and consolidated the mountain and western approaches. The immediate danger of the Turkish Cypriot community being crushed had been broken, while the Greek Junta and the Sampson government had both fallen during the crisis.

But the solution of the Cyprus question could no longer be found through another hill, village or road.

With the frontlines finally frozen and Geneva I coming to a close, the military phase was over. What followed would be slower, more complicated and perhaps even more dangerous in its own way. Turkey would now have to turn the military position created by Atilla I into a permanent political settlement through a long game of diplomacy...

part: PART III, GENEVA I: FULL CEASEFIRE-COMPLIANCE PATH
title: July 23, 1974, Orders must reach the militias
body:
The military intervention had already triggered consequences which few in Ankara could have imagined a week before. The very same Greek military junta which had ruled Greece for the previous seven years and which had organized the coup against Makarios was now crumbling under the pressure of the events in Cyprus. The commanders in Athens, who did not want to risk a war with Turkey which they were hardly prepared to fight, finally decided to return power to the civilian politicians and Konstantinos Karamanlis was called back from exile to form a new government. On the island itself, Nikos Sampson had been forced to step down as well and the new president was Glafkos Clerides.

These developments were very much welcomed in Ankara. Prime Minister Ecevit had repeatedly stressed that our intervention was aimed against the Greek military regime and its plans to realize Enosis, and not against the independence of Cyprus itself. Now that the juntas were gone, there was a real possibility to reach an agreement with the new Greek authorities without another confrontation between our two countries.

But the situation on the island was still rather different from the political turns in Athens and in Nicosia. The ceasefire which had been agreed upon on July 22 had formally ended the military operation but Greek Cypriot formations and irregular militias were still active all around the island. The collapse of Sampson's government had not suddenly established effective control over any of the armed groups while many Turkish villages were still left isolated and vulnerable to new attacks.

Our government thus demanded that Karamanlis and Clerides immediately bring order to the Greek and Greek Cypriot forces making sure that the orders to cease fighting would actually be obeyed. It would be rather pointless to declare an end to the hostilities between the regular armies while the irregular formations continued attacking Turkish settlements.

Meanwhile, our soldiers were ordered to reinforce the positions secured during the operation, prepare defensive lines, organize the supplies and reinforce the exposed points, but were not allowed to make any further progress. We had accepted the ceasefire and wanted to demonstrate that Turkey was willing to respect it as long as the other side fulfilled their part of the deal as well.

The military intervention had been successful in toppling the regime which had provoked the crisis. It was now the task of the new authorities to make sure that the fighting which the junta had launched would finally come to an end.

part: PART III, GENEVA I: FULL CEASEFIRE-COMPLIANCE PATH
title: July 24, 1974, Protection for Turkish villages
body:
Despite the restoration of civilian governments in Athens and Nicosia, reports reaching Ankara from Cyprus continued to cause our government significant concern. The ceasefire had now been in place for nearly two days, but many Turkish villages remained outside the area of control of our armed forces, surrounded by Greek Cypriot settlements and exposed to the activity of armed groups whose allegiance to the new authorities remained uncertain.

To Ecevit, this was becoming one of the main problems of the whole ceasefire arrangement. Our government had agreed to halt the advance of the Turkish army, but had never accepted that this meant abandoning the Turkish Cypriots who remained outside our military area. The intervention had been conducted in order to protect the community as a whole, not just those who had been so fortunate as to live within the territory which our soldiers had managed to secure.

The United Nations Security Council had now adopted Resolution 354, renewing its call for a ceasefire to be respected. Ankara welcomed the emphasis upon ending hostilities, but argued that the United Nations Peacekeeping Force must also be responsible for the security of the Turkish settlements which continued to face threats. The removal of armed formations from Turkish villages, protection of civilians and effective supervision of local ceasefire arrangements were all now becoming significantly important demands of our government.

There was also the bothersome matter of Nicosia Airport. During the previous days, the approach of Turkish forces towards the airport was nearly enough to bring our army into confrontation with the United Nations Peacekeeping Force, while Britain had reacted very hostilely to any possibility of the installation falling under Turkish control. Another such confrontation would have achieved little beyond worsening our relations with the very countries whose cooperation we now needed.

Our troops would now respect the existing arrangements and leave the airport to the United Nations. The positions surrounding our military perimeter would continue to be reinforced, but no attempt would be made to occupy the airport or expand into the surrounding territory.

With the Geneva Conference approaching, Turkey had decided to place its immediate demands upon the diplomatic table rather than seek further gains in territory. If Britain and the United Nations genuinely wanted to preserve the ceasefire, then they would have to ensure it protected the Turkish villages as well as the Greek positions facing our army.

A ceasefire which only stopped the Turkish soldiers, while leaving the Turkish civilians exposed to attack, could hardly be regarded as a satisfactory peace.

part: PART III, GENEVA I: FULL CEASEFIRE-COMPLIANCE PATH
title: July 25, 1974, Geneva I begins
body:
Finally, the First Geneva Conference opened. Turan Güneş led our delegation. The foreign ministers of Turkey, Greece, and Britain were trying to bring the situation in Cyprus under control. George Mavros had come from the new Greek government. James Callaghan, the British foreign secretary, had become very involved in organizing the talks. The Americans were also keeping a close eye on the situation, especially William Buffum, who had been sent by Kissinger.

Our goal was to avoid any further operations by the Turkish Army. We did not feel that merely drawing a line between the two sides would resolve the fundamental problems. The Turkish Cypriots had been living like this for over a decade, and the constitutional agreements of 1960 had not addressed these issues. The recent coup had also highlighted how precarious the situation was.

Güneş wanted to ensure that Turkish villages outside our military positions, especially those being attacked, occupied, or restricted by Greek Cypriot armed forces, would be protected. We asked the British and Americans to ensure that pressure was applied to the new governments in Athens and Nicosia so that all forces on the ground would respect the ceasefire.

Generally, relations were not great. Mavros was anxious about the Turkish military staying on the ground permanently. Callaghan wanted a statement to assure the international community that fighting had ceased.

We decided to try our best to find a diplomatic solution. The army was told to stay put, but extra troops and supplies were sent.

We will have to wait and see what more comes from the conference.

part: PART III, GENEVA I: FULL CEASEFIRE-COMPLIANCE PATH
title: July 26, 1974, Violations must be recorded
body:
July 26, 1974 – Breaches

The second day of the First Geneva Conference had begun, and there were tensions between our delegation and the Greeks.

There had been many breaches of the ceasefire by the Greek Cypriot military, particularly in Turkish villages that remained cut off from the areas our army had secured during the intervention. Our delegation expressed our concerns about this and said that the new government in Nicosia needed to be held accountable for the actions of the National Guard and irregular forces on the island.

However, the Greeks were concerned about our soldiers. Mavros still insisted that we needed to stop the Turkish army from advancing and asked when we would tell our soldiers to retreat to the line they held at the time of the original ceasefire.

Güneş reminded the other delegations that Turkey had agreed to the ceasefire on the understanding that it would be respected by both parties. We could hardly be expected to restrain our soldiers while ignoring armed groups that continued to threaten Turkish villages.

The Turkish delegation suggested that we could investigate the breaches with the help of the UN peacekeeping force. We would have to look into the advances made by the enemy, the situation in Turkish villages, and the activities of armed groups in these areas to ensure a lasting ceasefire.

If the conference does not come up with a way of investigating breaches, then the ceasefire will be nothing more than an agreement between foreign ministers.

part: PART III, GENEVA I: FULL CEASEFIRE-COMPLIANCE PATH
title: 27–28 July 1974, Evidence from the villages
body:
After several days of negotiations in Geneva, it was clear that there was scope for an agreement among the three countries, even though there were large differences between the Turkish and Greek delegations. Kissinger had ensured that the Greeks did not withdraw from the talks.

However, we were receiving some very troubling news from Cyprus.

There were still occupied settlements controlled by Greek Cypriot armed forces. There were also villages surrounded by armed forces with questionable intentions. The collapse of Sampson's government had not immediately brought about any sense of order, and the Turkish Cypriots outside our lines were still suffering.

Güneş outlined what he had learned from the villages. We had previously agreed that the army would not advance any further, so it would be hard for the Greeks to argue that the Turkish intervention was the only thing stopping peace. But they could not ignore the problems in the villages.

The Turkish delegation wanted all armed forces out of Turkish settlements and reliable ceasefire arrangements in place within the local areas. The vulnerable villages needed to be protected by the United Nations Peacekeeping Force. Any incidents outside the main military lines would need to be looked into. The treatment of civilians and prisoners taken during the fighting would also need to be dealt with quickly.

As the talks continued between Güneş, Mavros, and Callaghan, we began to draft a joint statement. Expert committees were set up to look at the proposals, including creating a security zone between the two military forces and determining what responsibilities UNFICYP would have in Turkish enclaves.

The Turks were reluctant to allow a security arrangement that would essentially leave us boxed in, with the villages outside our control. The Greeks were worried that if they agreed to a different security arrangement for the Turkish settlements, then the island would become permanently divided.

Our main worries were whether the Greeks would agree to the arrangements and whether the United Nations would have the ability to enforce them.

part: PART III, GENEVA I: FULL CEASEFIRE-COMPLIANCE PATH
title: 29–30 July 1974, Geneva I concludes
body:
The First Geneva Conference was drawing to a close. After nearly a week of intense negotiations, it looked like an agreement had been reached among the three delegations. However, although major issues had been resolved concerning the immediate ceasefire, there were still major arguments over the wording of the declaration.

Güneş had strict orders not to allow any clauses that could be seen as requiring an unconditional withdrawal. Callaghan was getting very frustrated with the constant complaints, and Mavros was constantly highlighting that the sovereignty and integrity of the Republic must be respected. There was every chance that the conference would fail to reach an agreement. At various points, it looked like no declaration would be signed.

However, the three delegations found a suitable solution. On July 30, the foreign ministers of Turkey, Greece, and Britain signed the Geneva Declaration, detailing the main agreements.

The agreement called for the areas controlled by opposing armed forces to remain as they were at 22:00 Geneva time on July 30. All forces, including irregular units, were called upon to stop attacking and engaging in hostile activity. A security zone would be created along the limits of the areas occupied by Turkish forces. The size of this zone would be determined during consultations between the three guarantor powers and the UN Peacekeeping Force. No forces other than UNFICYP would be permitted to enter this area.

The most important parts of the agreement for us were the sections concerning the Turkish villages. All Turkish enclaves occupied by Greek or Greek Cypriot forces would be immediately evacuated. Turkish enclaves outside the areas controlled by our army would continue to be protected by the United Nations. The Turkish communities would keep their existing local policing and security arrangements. Security in mixed villages would be handled by UNFICYP.

Military personnel and civilians detained during the recent conflict would be exchanged or released under the supervision of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

However, the most important issue remained unresolved:

The three guarantor nations agreed to start fresh negotiations on August 8. Turkish and Greek Cypriot representatives would be invited to discuss the political structure of the Republic. It was acknowledged that there were two autonomous administrations on the island in practice.

With the signing of the Geneva Declaration, the ceasefire that ended the First Cyprus Peace Operation now had a diplomatic framework.

Not one of the Greeks, British, Americans, or UN representatives had expected us to be so firm in our stance. Even less had they expected our military to be so bold. The Greek junta and Sampson's gamble had failed spectacularly for the Greeks. Our Turkish soldiers marched proudly across the plains and hills of Cyprus once again! Not only have we defeated the Greek and Greek Cypriot forces we faced, we have gained the upper hand in the north. The Greeks and the world are starting to realize that we could march our way across the island if we weren't holding back!

The result of this campaign cannot be underestimated. Atilla will go down in history and be studied in military academies for decades to come as one of the most daring military operations of the second half of the 20th century. Our military is gaining more respect and admiration. Our government (and therefore our party) has been revitalized more than ever before! We are finally being seen as true heirs to our father, Atatürk, and his party. Our leadership has shown our people that when the Empire fell and foreign powers attempted to destroy and split us up, it was thanks to Atatürk and his Society for the Defense of Rights of Anatolia and Rumelia that they were stopped! When Hatay was left under French rule, it was thanks to the efforts of Atatürk and his CHP that it was eventually returned! Now, when the lives of Turks in Cyprus were in danger, it was thanks to the party left behind by Atatürk that they were saved! Let them all know that no one can teach the CHP what being a nationalist really means!

Atilla and the First Geneva Conference had come to an end. The military aspect had come to a close. What came next would be longer, more complicated, and possibly even more dangerous. Turkey needed to turn its military victory into a lasting political solution through a long game of diplomacy...

Mavros, like Güneş, wanted the conference to end with a signature. He held out his hand.

“Agreed, Mr. Güneş.”

It was hard to believe, but the First Geneva Conference had truly ended...

part: PART III, GENEVA I: FULL CEASEFIRE-COMPLIANCE PATH
note: Original in-game July 31 text (the verbatim previous expanded rewrite was not recoverable)
title: 31 July 1974, The declaration must be implemented
body:
Turkey confirms that the decisions of Geneva I and the ceasefire will be fully implemented. Its troops will hold their positions, while the delegations prepare for the next conference.

Between August 1 and 8, there will be four diplomatic turns. Use the British and American flags to improve their attitudes towards Turkey. Every diplomatic action, or Skip 2 Days, uses one turn.

part: PART IV, GENEVA II: COMMON EVENTS
title: 8–9 August 1974, Geneva II begins
body:
The Second Geneva Conference had finally commenced. After much tension, the Turkish delegation met with the Greek and British delegations to continue discussing the fate of Cyprus. Many of the decisions made during the First Conference hadn’t been properly put into practice, and the ceasefire issue remained a contentious topic. Frontline, POW, and security issues were therefore assigned to expert committees, while the negotiations focused on the main issue: the constitution of Cyprus.

Turkey no longer believed it could return to the previous constitution. Over the past eleven years, culminating in the Greek coup and our military intervention, it had become clear that the Turkish community could no longer rely on the goodwill of the Greek Cypriot authorities to protect them. A new system needed to be created which would provide them with true autonomy.

Once again the Greeks were causing tension. Mavros, the Greek Foreign Minister, was opposed to discussing any constitutional issues until Denktaş and Clerides arrived. He stated that both communities should be represented.

Turan Güneş was becoming frustrated. We had called a second conference to discuss the constitution, but the Greeks seemed intent on delaying this process. We had spent weeks trying to come to an agreement and there was little reason to believe that by wasting more time we would get any closer to an agreement.

However, we now had Denktaş and Clerides, and this could be the chance to come to some sort of settlement if the Greeks would finally agree to something other than restoring the old order...

part: PART IV, GENEVA II: COMMON EVENTS
title: 10 August 1974, Two communities, five parties
body:
The Second Geneva Conference was only getting started when another issue was raised between our delegation and the Greeks. As you can imagine, this was a simple question but with major implications for the negotiations. Should Denktaş and Clerides represent two separate communities, or be treated as part of one delegation?

If we were to accept the latter, we would be acknowledging that the Greek Cypriot administration was the only legitimate authority on the island. This is something we had been fighting against for over a decade. After a lot of arguing, we were able to form a five-party conference. This meant that Turkey, Greece, Britain, Denktaş, and Clerides would each have their own representation.

However, this didn’t really help us overcome some of the larger issues. Turkey and Denktaş still wanted to form a federal solution based on partition. This would allow the Turkish community to govern their own land and protect themselves from any future attacks on their constitutional rights.

Clerides claimed that the 1960 Constitution was still in force and there was no need to change it. He also claimed that we couldn’t impose a constitutional agreement while Turkish troops occupied parts of the island. This was supported by Mavros as well as the rather disappointing British Foreign Minister Callaghan.

We didn’t agree with this. What point would there be in intervening and negotiating if we were just going to put the constitutional agreement back in place? We couldn’t expect the Turkish community to go back to how things were before.

However, the conference wasn’t completely at a standstill. Denktaş and Clerides agreed to meet privately the next day, away from the arguments between the three guarantor powers. They hoped they would be able to come to an agreement between the two communities.

Whether they would succeed where the foreign ministers had failed remained to be seen...

part: PART IV, GENEVA II: COMMON EVENTS
title: 11 August 1974, Another meeting without agreement
body:
The long-awaited private meeting between Denktaş and Clerides had finally taken place. However, the talks proved to be another dead-end. The Greek Cypriot side still refused to accept a geographical separation, while Denktaş refused to compromise on returning to the constitutional arrangements which had failed to protect his community.

This caused increasing frustration in Ankara. Bülent Ecevit, who had originally hoped that the military intervention would force the Greeks to accept the new political order in Cyprus, was getting impatient. He made it clear that Turkey was not going to spend valuable time and resources on a military operation only to revert to what we had before the coup. If the Greeks continued to refuse to compromise, our army was more than willing to resume operations.

However, interestingly enough, the Americans came up with an idea. Henry Kissinger was worried that Turkey would launch another offensive which would cause problems for the relationship between the two NATO allies. He suggested that perhaps the solution did not have to involve a bicommunal division of the island, and that autonomy could instead be given to the Turkish community in various regions within a federal Cyprus.

Turan Güneş thought this was a very sensible suggestion. Our main aim was to secure the autonomy of the Turkish Cypriots, so there was no real need to try to create one large territory in the north. This would give us another way of achieving our demands and also help avoid some of the objections to the Denktaş Plan.

This was the first new possibility that had come up since the start of Geneva II. Whether the Greeks would agree to this was another question, but with Ecevit's patience wearing thin and our army still waiting on the island to resume operations, there was not much time left to debate.

part: PART IV, GENEVA II: COMMON EVENTS
title: 12 August 1974, Two plans on the table
body:
The most critical point of the Second Geneva Conference had been reached. After many disputes, delays and disagreements over the constitutional future for Cyprus, Turan Güneş presented two distinct plans that could be used as the basis for a new political settlement. Both plans involved creating a federal Cyprus, but with two very different arrangements for Turkish autonomous areas.

The first plan was the Denktaş Plan. This plan had been what the Turkish delegation had wanted throughout the crisis. Cyprus would be split into two federal regions. The Turkish community would have a clearly defined area to administer in the north of the island while the Greek community would run the southern region. This would create two clearly defined areas, each with its own administration.

The second plan, partly inspired by Kissinger’s suggestion and proposed by Turan Güneş, took a different approach. Instead of creating one Turkish region in the north of the island, it would create six autonomous cantons for the Turkish community throughout the island. This meant that the Turkish community would have autonomy within a federal republic.

The British Foreign Minister, Callaghan, instantly commented on this. He stated that the Denktaş Plan would never be acceptable to the Greek Cypriots as they still saw this as an unacceptable outcome to the Turkish intervention. However, he also suggested that this second plan may be acceptable to the Greek Cypriot delegation. This meant there was now a possibility of us reaching an agreement after it looked like it would never happen.

However, would this actually be possible? Our relationship with the Western powers had deteriorated greatly during the military operations. Therefore it was unlikely that we would gain any support from Britain or America just because we had presented them with a more moderate option. The opinions of both countries, particularly the United States, which had great influence over the Greeks, would play a large role in whether this plan would work.

We were now faced with a difficult decision. We could continue to push for the Denktaş Plan with the hope of gaining geographical separation as we originally wanted. However, the Greeks and British were becoming increasingly determined not to let this happen. Alternatively, we could go for the Güneş Plan and accept that the Turkish community would have a different form of autonomy, in the hope that the Western powers would give us their support and lead to a peaceful settlement.

The army had done its part to change the situation on the island. It now depended on our diplomats to create a lasting solution from this based on whether we went for the first or second plan...

part: PART V, GENEVA II: DENKTAŞ PLAN REJECTED
title: 13 August 1974, The demand for more time
body:
The Second Geneva Conference had entered what seemed to be its most crucial hours. Though the Turkish delegation had made every possible effort to obtain a federal settlement based on geographical separation, the Greek Cypriot representatives had firmly opposed the Denktaş Plan and had refused to accept a separate Turkish region on the northern part of the island.

This had significantly hampered the conference's proceedings. Accepting the Denktaş Plan would have meant accepting a permanent division of Cyprus under the pressure of the Turkish army, and the Greek Cypriots were not ready to accept this, no matter how precarious their military position was. However, our delegation maintained that the events of the previous eleven years had proved that returning to the old constitutional arrangements was impossible, and geographical autonomy was a necessity if the Turkish community was to be protected from another crisis.

The talks grew increasingly contentious as the hours passed, with neither of the delegations willing to give an inch. The accusations hurled at one another by the delegates became so harsh that the conference was forced to conclude its day's proceedings prematurely, without any agreement being reached.

The situation was becoming rather tense. The Greeks had refused our main demands, and our government had made it clear that the military situation on the island could not remain as it was indefinitely. With neither of the sides willing to concede anything, an agreement with the use of the Denktaş Plan seemed to grow more and more distant with each hour that passed.

And the possibility of another Turkish military operation seemed to be growing with every passing hour...

part: PART V, GENEVA II: DENKTAŞ PLAN REJECTED
title: 14 August 1974, Clear answers
body:
The Second Geneva Conference had finally concluded, and despite days of negotiations, arguments and attempts to find a common ground between the two communities, the Greek Cypriot delegation had been firm in the belief that the Denktaş Plan had been rejected. Our demands for a geographically autonomous Turkish region in the north had been refused, while the Greeks continued to insist that the constitutional order established in 1960 was the only possible option upon which the future of Cyprus could be decided.

These events had stirred feelings of anger and disappointment in Ankara. Our government had launched a military intervention, risking a confrontation with Greece and enduring growing pressure from the Western powers, in order to ensure that the Turkish Cypriot community would never again find itself in the position it had suffered over the previous eleven years. Yet after almost a month of fighting and diplomacy, the Greeks were still refusing to accept the territorial arrangements that we had considered vital to their security.

For Ecevit and the General Staff, the situation was becoming increasingly unacceptable. Our army had been reinforced throughout the ceasefire and was now in a much more advantageous state than it had been during the first landings. If diplomacy had failed to secure our objectives, there remained the option of resuming the operation and establishing the territorial settlement through the use of military might. However, such a move would most probably lead to another wave of condemnations from Britain and America, whose relations with Turkey had suffered greatly during the crisis.

There was, however, another possibility. We could abandon our demands for geographical separation and reopen negotiations over a new version of the 1960 Constitution, seeking stronger political representation, administrative rights and security guarantees for the Turkish community inside a united Cypriot republic. Such a settlement would be significantly below our original goals, but could allow us to put an end to the crisis without another military operation.

We, therefore, were faced with perhaps the most important decision since our soldiers had first landed on the island. Should we order the continuation of Atilla, taking in the international consequences in order to set up the territorial security of the Turkish community, or should we give diplomacy another try, even though it would mean abandoning the geographical settlement for which we had fought?

part: PART VI, GENEVA II: GÜNEŞ PLAN, FAILED AND SUCCESSFUL PATHS
title: 13 August 1974, The demand for more time
body:
The Second Geneva Conference had entered what seemed to be the most crucial of its phases. Despite the Turkish delegation's efforts to establish a federal settlement of sorts through the Güneş Plan, a scheme which would divide Cyprus up into six geographically separate autonomous Turkish cantons, the Greek Cypriot representatives had shown no willingness to give a definite answer. Instead, Clerides and the Greek delegation demanded a further thirty-six to forty-eight hours to fully consider the proposal and consult their governments.

This demand, however, had done little to improve the atmosphere of the conference. To the Greek Cypriots, the Güneş Plan signified a major departure from the constitutional arrangements of 1960, and one which they were certainly unprepared to accept under the pressures of the Turkish army. Our delegation, meanwhile, held to the position that the events of the previous eleven years had proven conclusively that returning to the old arrangements was an impossibility, and that geographical autonomy was, in any case, a necessity if the Turkish community was to be safeguarded from another crisis.

As we proceeded into further talks, the arguments between the two delegations became increasingly heated. Turan Güneş refused to accept another postponement, insisting that the delegates could contact their governments directly, and reminding us that the constitutional question had been the very reason for summoning the Second Geneva Conference. We had already spent weeks attempting to reach an agreement, and there was no reason whatsoever to believe that giving either party thirty-six or forty-eight more hours would end the disagreements which had been outstanding for over a decade. Güneş warned that accepting such delays could result in turning the present crisis into years of further negotiations, never reaching a satisfactory settlement.

A rather dangerous situation was beginning to unfold. Although Kissinger had encouraged our government to consider a multi-zone federal arrangement, the political conditions necessary to obtain American support were clearly not in place. Our relations with Washington had deteriorated far too considerably for the Americans to openly support the Güneş Plan, and consequently, the anticipated meeting between Turan Güneş and Kissinger was not going to take place. Without the diplomatic backing of America, there was little hope of persuading the British to apply any additional pressure upon the Greek delegation. Our government had already made it clear that the military situation on the island could not go on indefinitely, and with the Greeks continuing to demand more time, the possibility of reaching an agreement via the Güneş Plan was growing ever more distant.

And with every passing hour, the prospects of another Turkish military operation were becoming harder and harder to ignore...

part: PART VI, GENEVA II: GÜNEŞ PLAN, FAILED AND SUCCESSFUL PATHS
note: Güneş Plan, Kissinger arranges support meeting
title: 13 August 1974, The demand for more time
body:
It appeared that the Second Geneva Conference was reaching its climax. Although the Turks had tried to reach a federal solution with the Güneş Plan, which proposed six geographically separate autonomous cantons for the Turkish community, the Greek Cypriots were still refusing to give a concrete answer. Clerides and the Greek delegation wanted more time to consider the plan and consult their governments. They asked for 36 to 48 hours.

This had created an extremely negative atmosphere. The Güneş Plan was very different from the constitution put in place in 1960 and the Greek Cypriots did not want to accept it under the pressure of the Turkish army. However, we argued that the past eleven years had shown that we could not go back to the old constitution and that the autonomous regions were needed to ensure the protection of the Turkish community.

Turan Güneş was very frustrated with the arguments and would not allow more time. He said that all delegations could contact their governments straight away. The reason that we were at the Second Geneva Conference was to discuss the constitution. We had been trying to reach an agreement for weeks. There was not much point in waiting another 36 or 48 hours when we already hadn’t resolved our differences in over a decade. He warned that if we granted more time, we could be stuck in endless negotiations for years to come with no good solution.

However, this time we were not arguing with the Greeks alone. Our military victories in Atilla I and our calm approach after the ceasefire had helped greatly improve our reputation in Washington. Kissinger, who had originally been quite reluctant to agree with our demands for separate regions, was starting to realize that any long-term solution would have to take into account the political and military facts.

He was very interested in the Güneş Plan. It had originally come up as a multizonal federation partly due to his suggestion. The fact that the Turkish government was willing to drop their demand for one continuous region showed the flexibility that Washington had been pushing for. The Turkish army had a large military advantage and the Greeks were not really willing to compromise, so Kissinger began to see the Turkish proposal as a sensible way to prevent another offensive.

It was Kissinger who arranged for the American delegation to speak with Turan Güneş later that day, to try and find a way for the American government to help.

Güneş explained that we had already compromised by dropping the Denktaş Plan and going for six separate autonomous cantons. However, the Greeks were still asking for more time with nothing to offer in return. We couldn’t expect our government to keep our army in those positions forever while the constitution remained unsettled.

Kissinger understood our points. He realized that the Turkish army could gain much more by force than Güneş was asking for diplomatically. If the talks failed again at Geneva then the consequences could be much bigger than just Cyprus. The Americans didn’t want to see two NATO allies getting into another conflict especially when we seemed to be close to a diplomatic solution.

After much discussion, Kissinger agreed to support the Güneş Plan. He realized that a multizonal solution would be a good basis for a federal solution. Washington would now try to use its diplomatic influence to get Britain on board with the plan and convince the Greeks that if they didn’t agree then they could end up in a much worse position.

This was a great achievement for us. The Greeks had been heavily relying on the pressure from the British and Americans to keep Turkey in check throughout the conference. However, things were starting to change. With Kissinger supporting our proposal, we could no longer assume that the Western powers would continue to back the Greeks.

However, just because the American Secretary of State agreed to the Güneş Plan didn’t mean that the Greeks agreed. We still needed to get Callaghan fully behind the plan and convince the Greeks that a federal solution was better than risking another Turkish military action.

Although we still hadn’t saved the conference, we had for the first time something more valuable than another promise of negotiations. We had the support of the United States and our army had already proved how strong it was.

Whether the Greeks would finally realize this...

part: PART VI, GENEVA II: GÜNEŞ PLAN, FAILED AND SUCCESSFUL PATHS
note: Güneş Plan, UK/US backing leads to Greek acceptance
title: 14 August 1974, Clear answers
body:
The Second Geneva Conference was at last reaching its most crucial point. After many exhausting days of arguing and constant threats of another Turkish military operation, Turan Güneş demanded clear answers to the proposals put forward by our government to the Greek Cypriot delegation.

Would the Greeks accept the new constitutional structure based on geographical areas? Would they accept that around 34% of Cyprus would be handed over to Turkish Cypriot rule within the federal system? Would they accept a security area to be set up to the west of the area currently held by our armed forces?

These were the basic requirements of a lasting settlement. We had already made very large concessions in order to reach this point. Having dropped our demand for a unified Turkish area, we had come to accept the Güneş Plan, which would give us six separate autonomous cantons. However, it seemed that there would be no real result from this if the Greeks continued to reject the idea of geographical autonomy.

However, after discussions with Turan Güneş through the American delegation, Henry Kissinger had agreed to back the multi-area federal structure. He had realized that Turkey had already made large concessions and if the talks failed again another military operation could begin. The Americans were fully aware of how much stronger our army was compared to the Greeks and there was little reason to believe that another attack would somehow benefit Greece or the West.

Kissinger therefore started to put much pressure on the British government. During discussions with Callaghan, he made it clear that the Güneş Plan was a good opportunity to resolve the crisis without another confrontation between two NATO countries. While the British could still continue to back the Greek requests for more time, if the conference failed and the Turkish army returned to military operations then things would become much harder to control.

Callaghan was not really keen to be in this situation. Throughout the conference the British had always pushed for the Turkish army to be kept in check and for Cyprus’s constitutional order to be maintained. They had also been very suspicious about our requests for land. However, with the Americans now backing the Turkish request, it would be hard for them to remain isolated. They would have little choice but to back the Turkish request as the alternative would be another military operation and London had little desire to stop this using force.

Eventually Callaghan agreed with Kissinger and decided that the Brits would back the Güneş Plan as a settlement. This meant that the British delegation started to join the Americans in pressuring the Greeks into dropping their tactic of stalling.

This immediately put the Greek delegation in a difficult position. They had previously relied on British support and American pressure on Turkey to resist our demands. However, both Western powers were now pushing for a settlement to be reached and neither seemed willing to take the risk of another Turkish attack just to gain more time.

Mavros and Clerides still voiced their concerns, especially about handing over such a large amount of land to Turkish Cypriot rule. They did not want to accept these terms as they would be admitting that the Republic had changed fundamentally due to the Turkish intervention. However, the pressure from London and Washington made it very difficult to refuse.

Throughout the morning the negotiations continued. The Greek delegates were actually discussing the Turkish proposals. The constitutional nature of the six cantons, the amount of territory to be ruled by Turkish Cypriots, and details of the security area were discussed. The Americans and British tried to iron out any remaining disputes.

Finally, just before midday...

The Greek delegation agreed to the three main demands put forward by Turan Güneş. They agreed to accept the Güneş Plan as the basis for a new federal settlement.

Ankara was delighted with this news. After nearly a month of military tension and difficult negotiations, we had reached a political settlement which would give the Turkish Cypriots geographical autonomy without needing to launch another offensive. Turkey had shown its commitment to defending its rights under the Treaty of Guarantee. Our diplomats had successfully turned the military situation into an agreement.

Most importantly, this agreement had the support of the British and Americans. Just a few days ago these countries had threatened Turkey with diplomatic repercussions if our army attacked again. However, thanks to the efforts of Güneş and Kissinger, they had helped to persuade the Greeks into accepting the seemingly impossible settlement.

Of course there was still a lot to do. The borders and administration of the six Turkish cantons needed to be decided. The appropriate federal structures needed to be set up. The security arrangements agreed upon at Geneva needed to be put into place. Our soldiers would stay where they were and there would be no more offensive operations.

However, the most dangerous part of the crisis was now over.

There would be no Second Cyprus Peace Operation. Turkey had managed to gain what it wanted through diplomacy rather than another advance. The future of Cyprus would now be decided based on the agreement being put into place.

Ecevit and Güneş had definitely earned themselves something to celebrate. The Turkish Cypriots had gained geographical autonomy which we felt was vital to their security. Cyprus had remained independent and there was a chance of coexistence.

After seemingly impossible negotiations, an agreement had been reached...

part: PART VI, GENEVA II: GÜNEŞ PLAN, FAILED AND SUCCESSFUL PATHS
title: 15 August 1974, From agreement to administration
body:
The news reached Ankara, and after a month of fighting, diplomacy and the prospect of another war, it was time to celebrate our government's success. The Greeks had accepted the Güneş Plan, and this meant we no longer needed to undertake the Second Cyprus Peace Operation. The six autonomous Turkish cantons would be formed within a federal Cyprus.

It was a huge success for our Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit. We had achieved our goal of protecting the Turkish Cypriots while avoiding war with Greece and criticism from our Western allies. Turan Güneş and his team had achieved a political victory through diplomacy.

However, the agreement still needed to be put into place. The Turkish, Greek and British governments, Denktaş, Clerides and the appropriate Cypriot institutions were officially notified. The UN would also oversee its implementation to ensure neither community broke the agreement.

Our troops were told to stay where they were on the ceasefire line. Civil servants began to draw up lists of settlements that would be handed over to the Turkish Cypriot administration. Officials began to set up the institutions for the six cantons.

Much work still needed to be done. We needed to discuss the exact borders of the cantons, their ties to the capital and the security guarantees. However, this would not mean that all the issues that had plagued Cyprus over the last eleven years would disappear.

The junta in Athens and Sampson's regime had been overthrown, and both Greece and Turkey were getting ready to help set up a new political structure in a federal Cyprus. Hopefully, the people of Cyprus could now move on with their lives without fearing any more violence. Instead of reading about another village being burned down, another attack or another failed agreement, hopefully we would soon be reading about peace between the Turkish and Greek communities.

part: PART VI, GENEVA II: GÜNEŞ PLAN, FAILED AND SUCCESSFUL PATHS
title: 21 August 1974, The northern canton
body:
Almost a week after the Güneş Plan was put into motion, the first results were showing. The largest of the six autonomous Turkish cantons had been created in northern Cyprus.

This was an exciting time for the Turkish communities. They were finally seeing the geographical autonomy that Denktaş and our government had been demanding. The administration in northern Cyprus would be run by Turkish Cypriots.

The Northern Canton was the main piece of land captured by our soldiers. We now had a military presence in place, which could be turned into a political structure. While the soldiers had done an incredible job capturing the area, our new civil administration could now take over.

Turkish Cypriot officials were beginning to get to grips with their new roles, with support from the guarantor powers and the UN. There was a lot more to do with the other five cantons.

Ankara had every reason to be happy. Although there had been criticism of our government for agreeing to something less than our original demand of one Turkish region, it was becoming clear that the Güneş Plan wasn't a 'giveaway'. Progress was already being made on the island.

Although Denktaş had spent most of his political career pushing for proper guarantees for his community, he now had the unique challenge of setting up the very administration he had fought for diplomatically. The Turkish Cypriot authorities would have to work together to ensure the cantons ran smoothly.

There were still challenges ahead. It would take time to rebuild relations between the two communities.

However, the largest canton had been set up. While there were still five to go, with each administration being established, the agreement that had looked so uncertain in Geneva was beginning to become a reality.

part: PART VI, GENEVA II: GÜNEŞ PLAN, FAILED AND SUCCESSFUL PATHS
title: 30 August 1974, The Güneş Plan is announced
body:
More than a month after the Turkish Armed Forces landed on the shores of Kyrenia, great political changes had occurred in Greece and Turkey. After the fall of the junta in Athens, the collapse of Sampson's government and two tough rounds of negotiations in Geneva, we had finally achieved a political settlement.

On this great day, August 30, 1974, the anniversary of our glorious victory in the War of Independence, we had some more great news to share with the Turkish nation.

The Güneş Plan was finally a reality!

The official agreement stated that Cyprus would become a federal republic consisting of six separate geographical Turkish cantons. Each canton would have its own administration.

This was a great victory for our Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit and Foreign Minister Turan Güneş. Despite the Greek delegation initially refusing to agree to any geographical separation and the British being reluctant to accept territorial autonomy, our military victory, Turkey's maintenance of the ceasefire and Kissinger's diplomatic efforts resulted in the Western powers backing the settlement.

Despite the Americans' initial worries about an open conflict between Turkey and Greece, they persuaded both the British and the Greek delegation to accept the plan. We weren't forced to give up our demand for Turkish Cypriot autonomy and didn't have to conquer all of Cyprus. However, the victory was made sweeter because our military didn't have to carry out the Second Cyprus Peace Operation.

part: PART VI, GENEVA II: GÜNEŞ PLAN, FAILED AND SUCCESSFUL PATHS
body:
WE DID IT!

After a month of struggling, after the puppet junta in Athens had tried to impose Enosis on Cyprus and the Turkish Cypriots had prepared themselves for yet another genocide, we managed to bring down the junta, keep Cyprus independent and give our Turkish community the autonomy they fought for.

We also avoided being internationally isolated and secured a deal backed by Britain and the USA due to our military successes. Turkey had shown that it could achieve its goals using a combination of military power and diplomacy.

The CHP was not far behind. We saw a huge increase in Ecevit's popularity, and we gained much ground in the polls. Confidence in our government had increased significantly thanks to our military victories, Güneş's determination in Geneva and our Prime Minister's leadership.

Most importantly, we could finally guarantee the Turkish Cypriots that they would never have to make the heartbreaking choice between staying in Cyprus under Greek Cypriot rule or leaving their homes and everything they knew to go to Turkey. Our communities would stay in Cyprus, with local councils running each of the six autonomous cantons.

Turkey had achieved everything it wanted without another attack, without leaving the Turkish Cypriots high and dry or giving up Cyprus to Enosis.

What more could our government have done?

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
title: August 14, 1974, Atilla II
body:
The Second Geneva Conference was finally closed on the morning of August 14. Our government made all efforts to convince the Greeks to accept the Cyprus settlement, including the separation of Cyprus according to the territorial integrity principle, but the Greek delegation did not agree to the separation of Cyprus lands, which Turkey demanded. Turan Bey, having realized that there was no point in further negotiations, ended the meeting when the Greek and British delegations were still insisting that negotiations had not yet reached an impasse.

Meanwhile, while the diplomats were busy arguing in Geneva, a completely different drama was unfolding in Cyprus. Our General Staff had completed all the preparations for the second operation, and the order to start attacking had come from the Adana command post in Turkey. The objective of the attack was the Şahin Line. The password was ZAFER.

Again on the morning of August 15 at 5:30 am, Turkish planes appeared in the skies of Cyprus. The first bombs were dropped on Greek positions, and nearly 40,000 Turkish soldiers and armored cars had crossed the border of Cyprus from the districts gained during Operation Atilla I. Unlike the first operation, during which our troops faced great difficulties capturing a bridgehead and connecting the landing points of the seaborne and airborne assaults, we greatly outnumbered the Greeks this time and had sufficient armor and firepower to launch a successful attack.

Our troops advanced both to the west and the east, attempting to widen the bridgehead and to extend it in the direction of Lefke and Mağusa. The first day of the operation was marked by the fiercest Greek resistance. Nevertheless, the morale of our troops was high, and they had managed to capture most of the strategically important communication centers. However, the resistance in most cases was not as massive as during the first operation when our troops had to fight their way to within the range of the howitzers brought by the airborne assault troops. Turkish tanks were now breaking through the front lines of the Greek defense, and the Greek troops had great difficulty standing their ground against the advancing armored columns.

At the same time, the local population in Cyprus had its share of worries. Thousands of Greek Cypriots had already fled their homes in the eastern part of the city when they had heard about the Turkish planes and armored cars rushing toward Mağusa. Although our government claimed that the Turkish Cypriot community was in great need of protection, as the enclaves where they lived were still within the territorial jurisdiction of Greece, the residents of these enclaves had to suffer the dangers of war as well.

It is worth noting that the international community was not very enthusiastic about the Turkish offensive, either. Britain, which was extremely frustrated by the failed negotiations in Geneva, was now trying to rally the opinion of the international community against Turkey. The UN Security Council called for an immediate ceasefire, and President Gerald Ford was doing his best to prevent the open conflict between NATO members. Meanwhile, Greece demanded the dissolution of NATO because this alliance was unable to protect Greece from Turkish aggression.

Thus, although the military situation facing Turkey seemed to be favorable, the political situation had deteriorated considerably. Our troops were making steady progress, heading for the strategically significant regions that had been previously unattainable for us. However, Britain and other NATO members were now making it clear that they would not tolerate unrestricted Turkish expansionism.

Operation Atilla II had begun, and this time our troops would not be satisfied with a narrow bridgehead. But how many more Turkish soldiers would have to die for Turkey to obtain the international recognition it sought?

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
title: August 15, 1974, Atilla II
body:
The second day of Atilla II had begun; our forces continued their advance both to the east towards Mağusa and to the west towards Lefke. Unlike the first operation, which had seen our soldiers fighting through heavily fortified lines of Greek forces in the Beşparmak Mountains, the Second Operation was proving to face little resistance. The Greek National Guard was proving unable to hold back our much larger Turkish army and was beginning to withdraw its lines as our armoured formations continued to secure the roads and settlements required to reach the Şahin Line.

By 18:00 Turkish tanks were approaching the outskirts of Mağusa, while our commando and airborne formations were surrounding the famous hotel and tourist district of Maraş which lay immediately to the south of the city. However, our army was advancing more slowly in this district, in order to allow the many foreign tourists and hotel staff to vacate the district before our soldiers entered it. The General Staff had also ordered that any Greek Cypriots wishing to vacate the territories coming under our control should be allowed to do so.

The effects of the operation were beginning to be seen among the civilian population. Thousands of Greek Cypriots were vacating their homes as the Turkish army drew closer, while the roads around Mağusa were filled with people desperately trying to get away from the advancing front. For the Turkish Cypriots who had been living in isolation within their enclaves since the previous weeks, the approach of our forces had given them hope that they could finally escape the dangers that they had been living under. However, for the many Greek Cypriots fleeing from the very same army, the intervention had proved to be a disaster which they would never forget.

Despite our success on the battlefield, our army was not completely free from the confusion which had plagued our first operation. The rapid advances of tanks and armoured vehicles had occasionally caused problems in coordination, and one such incident close to the British military base at Dikelya had nearly resulted in an entirely new international crisis. American officials, who had been keeping watch on the advances of Turkish formations, warned Ankara that some of our units were dangerously close to the British base. The warning was followed by British protests, and military headquarters in Adana immediately ordered the troops involved to vacate the area.

A crisis of this nature was a stark reminder of the precarious diplomatic position in which Turkey now found itself. Britain led the charge against our continued advances, while in Washington the American Congress was beginning to demand an arms embargo against Turkey. Congressman John Brademas, one of the most vocal protestors of the intervention, confronted Kissinger on the issue of American weapons being used by our forces and called for military assistance to be cut until the Turkish army withdrew. While Kissinger did not seem to be overly bothered by the issue, feeling that the political cost of an embargo would outweigh any satisfaction it might bring to the Greeks, not all of those in the American administration shared his confidence.

With Greece announcing its withdrawal from NATO's military structure and the Turkish army still advancing, Washington was growing increasingly wary of the prospect of another confrontation between the two nations. American officials were calling for an immediate ceasefire and return to negotiations before the situation got any worse.

For our government, the military progress had been little different. The advances to the east and west had meant the narrow corridor secured during Atilla I had begun to widen into an area much more easily defended, while the great positions of the Greeks had failed to provide the resistance our commanders had originally feared.

However, although the army was approaching the objectives it had desired, the international consequences of the operation were becoming considerably more serious. Britain was openly hostile, criticism was coming from the American Congress and the United Nations continued to press for an end to the hostilities.

Our forces were now approaching the final boundaries of the operation. It remained to be seen whether the army could complete the advance before the Western powers succeeded in forcing yet another ceasefire...

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
note: Confirmation prompt: extend offensive by 14 hours
title: Are you sure?
body:
Our army has fulfilled the task designated for the Second Cyprus Peace Operation. We have taken the line of Mağusa–Lefke, and the Turkish Cypriots have been given a substantial and well-defended territory, which seemed impossible to achieve when our troops first landed on Cyprus. The General Staff is ready to agree to a ceasefire at 18:00, thus terminating military operations.

In the opinion of our commanders, another fourteen-hour operation up to 08:00 tomorrow could yield significant results, particularly, the capture of Nicosia Airport, which was beyond our reach during the confrontation with the British in July.

But at what cost might such a decision be purchased? Britain has already warned of military confrontations over the issue of the airport, while the United States has grown increasingly hostile to our continued expansion. The United Nations is calling for an immediate ceasefire, and economic sanctions and a deterioration of the exchange situation may inflict considerable damage on our economy.

We have already attained our goal, and another fourteen-hour offensive might transform our victory into a diplomatic and economic defeat, the consequences of which our country would have to bear for a long time.

Is it worth risking all of this for the sake of another fourteen hours of warfare?

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
title: Report
body:
With the objectives of the Second Cyprus Peace Operation finally achieved, our government has ordered the Turkish Armed Forces to cease their offensive operations at 18:00. The Mağusa–Lefke line has been secured and our army now controls approximately 38% of Cyprus, giving our Cypriot community a large, defendable territory in the north.

The battles had finally ended. Despite the considerable pressure Britain, America and the United Nations had put on us, our forces have succeeded in securing the territorial position they were trying to push for, the one the Geneva negotiations failed to provide. The army would remain in its positions; no further advances would be made.

Atilla II has ended; the final military and diplomatic settlement report will arrive in two days, when our government must decide what is to become of the territories we have secured.

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
title: Report
body:
Despite the General Staff having achieved its principal objectives, our government has decided to postpone the ceasefire for another fourteen hours. The army has been ordered to continue its operations until 08:00 on August 17, allowing our commanders to achieve further territorial gains before bringing the Second Cyprus Peace Operation to an end.

But the decision has already caused considerable alarm amongst our allies! The United Nations has demanded an immediate halt to hostilities, whilst Britain and America had expected our forces to halt at the Mağusa–Lefke line. Our advances in and around Nicosia Airport have risked bringing Turkey into confrontation with those powers which will be relied upon to cooperate with us once the operation has ended.

The ceasefire will now come into effect at 08:00 tomorrow. Our army has fourteen more hours to improve its positions, but the consequences of this decision could affect far more than the battlefront...

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
note: Alternative final day: Nicosia Airport captured
title: August 17, 1974, Atilla II
body:
The Second Cyprus Peace Operation had already achieved its goals set by the General Staff, but our government decided to continue the attack for another fourteen hours. The ceasefire was scheduled to begin at 08:00, but Turkish troops penetrated well beyond the Mağusa-Lefke line, in an effort to secure additional objectives before the operation’s end.

The most critical objective of the Second Operation was the Nicosia airport.

The possession of the airport had been a matter of contention between Turkey and Britain since the First Operation in July. When our airborne troops were approaching the airport, the British foreign minister Callaghan even threatened Turkey with British military action. At the same time, the UN Security Council called upon both nations to leave the airport’s possession to international authorities. Nevertheless, our government did not attempt to capture the facility at that time, as such an action would have resulted in an immediate confrontation with Britain.

Now, with the whole of Northern Cyprus under our control and Greek defenses already disintegrated, the capture of the Nicosia airport seemed a logical continuation of the operation. Turkish troops pressed forward, undeterred by Britain’s diplomatic protests, and managed to occupy the airport before the ceasefire was enforced at 08:00.

With our troops capturing Nicosia airport, the area of our territorial claims jumped to 42 percent. It significantly exceeded the goals set by our government for the Second Operation. Thus, from a purely military perspective, it can be said that the continuation of the operation beyond the initial goals was justified. The area secured by our troops surpassed even the targets set by the General Staff at the beginning of the fighting, which commenced on July 20. The Northern Cyprus region was entirely under our control, and we also captured strategic positions that would give us leverage in the future negotiations.

Nevertheless, the military success failed to achieve its diplomatic goals.

The immediate reaction to the further advancement of our troops came in the form of criticism from Britain’s foreign minister Callaghan. He condemned our capture of Nicosia airport, which he viewed as an attempt to revise the settlement favored by the UN Security Council. At the same time, the American government was growing impatient with the Turkish leadership as well. The US President Ford grew increasingly concerned about Turkey’s insistence on immediate withdrawal of Greek troops from Cyprus.

We had jeopardized the support from Washington by advancing beyond the designated limits. The arguments presented by the US administration no longer held water, as the military goals of the operation were already achieved when the Northern Cyprus region was captured. The calls upon international law and NATO alliance were no longer convincing to either Britain or the US.

The diplomatic isolation of Turkey was soon reinforced by another development, as the economic sanctions regime was imposed on our country. The sanctions hit the foreign exchange balance, further complicating the situation of our economy.
