The growing economic difficulties ahead of the military ones will make the already precarious situation of our economy even worse. Our economy, which relied so heavily on foreign investments, imports, and international ties, was now threatened by another crisis.

The domestic front in Turkey was not celebrating the victories either, as the triumph was overshadowed by many negative aspects. Even as the military successes of our troops reassured the domestic public, the foreign policy miscalculations of our government made many people realize that the country was advancing toward a dead end. The domestic critics of the war argued that although our troops did capture new regions, these successes came at too high of a price. Meanwhile, our government seemed to fail to understand this, and continued to engage in adventurism.

Thus, on August 17 at 08:00, fourteen hours after the original ceasefire deadline, the ceasefire was declared.

Atilla II ended as a spectacular success for our troops. They achieved remarkable feats of arms, but the price of this success was exceedingly high. The foreign policy blunders committed by our government threatened to undermine the military successes achieved. The future of our country, and the foreign policy course adopted by our government, was uncertain.

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
title: Report
body:
The long-awaited ceasefire has finally taken place at 08:00. After fourteen hours of fighting, our troops captured Nicosia Airport and managed to occupy 42 percent of Cyprus, greatly increasing the region under Turkish control beyond the projected goals of the Second Operation.

Nevertheless, it has considerably strained our foreign policy with both Britain and America, who have expressed their disapproval of our actions, and has lowered our international reputation by one level. Moreover, immediate economic sanctions have been imposed on the Turkish economy, further pressuring the exchange rates and reserves.

Atilla II is over. Our armed forces will hold the territory captured during the offensive, including the Nicosia Airport, but any further attacks or advances will be strictly prohibited by the Turkish command.

While we have exceeded our initial gains on the battlefield, the future of the Cyprus conflict remains uncertain. The final report on the settlement terms is due in two days, and our government will have to formulate a plan to turn the current gains into a lasting territorial reward under significantly more difficult conditions.

part: PART VII, ATILLA II AND THE TWO CEASEFIRE OUTCOMES
note: Atilla II victory outcome, extended-offensive path
body:
Our army has achieved its goals in Cyprus! What began on 20 July as an uncertain landing on the narrow beaches of Kyrenia has ended in Turkish troops occupying an extensive area from Mağusa to Lefke, and with the addition of gains on the final day, even Nicosia Airport had fallen to us. The Turkish-Cypriot community, which for eleven long years had lived in the shadow of violence and persecution, would from now on not have to depend on the goodwill of the authorities in Nicosia for its survival.

The news of our success had sparked celebrations all across Turkey. The soldiers, sailors and airmen who had fought on the island were hailed as heroes, and Prime Minister Bülent Ecevit, increasingly seen by many as the man who had finally solved the Cyprus question by force of arms where diplomacy had failed, had seen his popularity skyrocket. For CHP, whose support had risen by five percent in the polls, the operation had proved to be perhaps the most successful political move by the government so far.

But at a great cost. Our decision to go beyond the original objectives, and the disregard of the British warnings when we captured Nicosia Airport were taking their toll on our relations with the Western world. Britain and America were openly criticizing our actions, and the economic sanctions imposed upon Turkey threatened to hurt our precarious foreign exchange situation. The very countries we had tried to enlist as allies at the Geneva Conferences were now turning against Ankara.

And even though our army had performed brilliantly, occupying large regions and securing a defensible front, it was clear that the political future of Cyprus was far from settled. We could hold territory and fortify positions, but we could not force the entire world to accept a permanent division of the island. If we wanted to achieve a federal solution based upon either the Denktaş or Güneş proposals, we would eventually have to return to negotiations, and mend our relations with America and the West.

We had won the war, but could we win the peace without betraying our conquests?

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
note: Turkey abandons territorial autonomy and opens constitutional talks
title: Report
body:
The atmosphere in the Second Geneva Conference has changed completely following our delegation's announcement that Turkey would no longer insist on the creation of a geographically autonomous Turkish region in Cyprus. The Greeks, who had been so strongly against Denktaş and Güneş proposals over the past days were incredibly relieved by our unexpected concession. Even Callaghan, who had been constantly saying that we will never be able to reach an agreement if Turkey insisted upon its territorial demands seemed much more optimistic than before.

But for us and our delegates, it was not really a time to celebrate. After nearly a month-long military campaign and intense negotiations, we had to give up one of the main objectives that our government pursued when it sent our delegation to Cyprus. Turkish Cypriots will have to look for their security and territorial integrity within the territorial integrity of a united republic, not in the autonomous region that Denktaş demanded.

However, all was not lost; the negotiations did not end in total failure. The five delegations agreed to hold discussions on a new constitution, study each of them for one day and try to adopt a new constitution which will ensure that the disputes and intercommunal violence which plagued Cyprus in the last eleven years will not be repeated.

Whether the Greeks would be more pliable now that we had given up our demand for an autonomous region would become clear in the next few days. We gave our concessions. Now it will be the time to see whether they really want an agreement, or if they only want to re-establish the old order under a different name...

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 14, 1974, Powers of the central government
body:
The Second Geneva Conference, which only a few hours before seemed set to collapse completely, was saved by an unexpected change in the position of the Turkish government. Our delegation gave up on demanding a geographical separation of the two communities, and agreed that a new constitutional arrangement would be negotiated so that Cyprus remained a single, united republic.

The decision was welcomed with considerable satisfaction by the Greek delegation, who had spent the previous days opposing practically every territorial proposal put forward by Turkey. However, this did not mean that an agreement suddenly became inevitable. If the Turkish Cypriots were to be scattered all over the island living under the same central government as the Greek majority, then there would have to be very clear limitations upon what that government could do.

The first issue was the distribution of authority between the central government and the two communities. Our delegation argued that the failure of the 1960 Constitution had shown that it was dangerous to leave such matters open to interpretation. The Greeks, however, argued that a sovereign Cypriot republic could not function properly if too many of the responsibilities were transferred to the communal institutions.

Three different arrangements had now come out of the talks.

Turkish proposal

Our delegation proposes that the powers of the central government should be individually listed out in the Constitution, leaving no room for the government to make up any additional authority on its own.

Foreign affairs, national defense, currency, customs, citizenship, foreign trade, national transportation and communications, and the basic management of public finances will be the responsibility of the central government.

However, education, culture, religion, personal status, municipal services and local development will be held under the authority of the respective community administrations, along with certain health and social services. In this way, the Turkish Cypriots will be able to conduct many of their daily affairs independently without having to rely on the decisions of the Greek majority.

Compromise

A slightly more centralized arrangement has also been proposed, under which the central government will be in charge of foreign affairs, defense, currency, citizenship, the national economy, customs and general taxation.

Education, culture, religion and personal status will be exclusively in the hands of the two communities, protecting their ability to preserve their own institutions and traditions.

However, municipal services, healthcare, local roads, housing and local development will be administered under a common legal framework established by the central government, and their implementation will be left to the local administrations.

Greek proposal

The Greek delegation insists that the general authority of the Republic must remain with the central state, and will be as expected of a united country.

Only a very limited number of responsibilities, namely education, religion, culture and personal status, will be constitutionally reserved for the two communities. All other matters will fall under the authority of the central government, unless provided otherwise.

Local administrations will continue to exist, but their powers will be delegated by the state instead of being independently guaranteed to the communities.

The issue before us was no longer where the Turkish community will administer its own territory, but how much authority it will possess within the institutions of a united Cyprus.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 15, 1974, The Turkish community’s political status
body:
The negotiations had now turned towards one of the principal disputes which had plagued the Republic of Cyprus since its establishment in 1960: the political position of the Turkish community within a state where the Greek Cypriots formed an overwhelming majority of the population.

Under the original constitutional arrangement, the Turkish Cypriots had been afforded a separate Vice-President, representation in the government and various constitutional protections designed to prevent the Greek majority from ruling the island completely on its own terms. Yet these provisions had also become the source of continuous disagreements, especially with regard to the exercise of veto powers and how far the Turkish community could go in thwarting legislation it saw as harmful to its interests.

For our delegation, abandoning the demand for territorial autonomy made this question even more pressing. The Turkish Cypriots would no longer have a separate geographical region within which they could exercise political authority. Their protection would therefore have to come from the institutions which had proved unable to prevent the constitutional crisis of 1963.

The Greeks were prepared to discuss a continuation of communal representation, but were firm in their opposition to restoring the extensive veto powers of the original Constitution.

Turkish proposal

The Turkish Vice-Presidency would be retained to ensure that the Turkish community still had an independent representative in the highest office of the Republic.

Turkish Cypriots would be guaranteed at least 20% representation in all institutions of the state, while representatives of the two communities would continue to be elected using separate electoral rolls.

Our delegation is prepared to lay down the general veto powers which had caused so many disagreements in the original Constitution. However, legislation affecting the constitutional status of the Turkish community, the powers of its local governments, language rights, education or security would have to be separately approved by the Turkish representatives.

In ordinary political affairs, the government could go on with its business without the constant threat of a veto. But when it came to the fundamental rights of the Turkish community, it would not be permitted to decide everything by itself.

Compromise

The Republic would retain a Greek Cypriot President and a Turkish Cypriot Vice-President, although the absolute veto powers established by the original Constitution would be abolished.

Parliament would be made up of approximately sixty Greek Cypriot and fifteen Turkish Cypriot representatives, elected by their respective communities using separate electoral rolls.

Ordinary legislation would be passed by a general parliamentary majority, but amendments to laws which specifically protected Turkish constitutional rights would require a reinforced majority which included the definite support of a fixed number of Turkish representatives.

This would give the Turkish community protection in relation to certain constitutional matters without re-establishing the system of absolute vetoes.

Further Greek proposal

Our delegation has refused to allow any further reduction in the political status of the Turkish community.

We have already laid down our demand for a geographically autonomous region. To accept an arrangement which would allow the Turkish Cypriots to be denied their constitutional protections by an ordinary parliamentary majority would leave them almost entirely at the mercy of the goodwill of the Greek majority.

There can be no further concession on this question.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 16, 1974, Local government
body:
The third day of constitutional negotiations had thrown up another contentious issue. Turkey had agreed to give up geographical separation, which meant that Turkish villages and municipalities scattered throughout Cyprus would have to remain in the same administrative structure as the Greek Cypriot settlements.

It was easy to agree to in principle, but more challenging to implement. The Turkish Cypriots had acquired their own communal institutions during the years of anarchy, and Denktaş was especially concerned that returning to a centralized system would allow the Greek administration to gradually erode these institutions.

Our delegation contended that it would be ridiculous to guarantee political representation in Nicosia while allowing the central government to interfere with nearly any local decision a Turkish village or municipality may take. Meanwhile, the Greek delegation was unwilling to accept the creation of what it saw as a second government existing alongside the Republic.

The dispute went beyond the powers of individual municipalities, as whether or not Turkish settlements should be permitted to organize themselves collectively even when separated by great distances was also in question.

Turkish proposal

Turkish villages and municipalities would be permitted to set up their own communal administrative groups, regardless of whether these settlements were geographically connected to one another.

These local administrations would be coordinated through a Turkish Community Assembly or a Local Administration Board, allowing the Turkish community to organize its municipal affairs across the country without requiring the establishment of a continuous Turkish territory.

The central government would retain sovereignty over the entirety of Cyprus; however, the constitutional powers granted to the Turkish local administrations could not be unilaterally revoked or withdrawn by the central state.

Compromise

Each village and municipality in Cyprus would have its own elected council which would handle local affairs.

Turkish settlements which were geographically close to one another, or had practical administrative needs, would be allowed to set up joint service unions to handle their common responsibilities.

However, there would be no separate island-wide Turkish administrative hierarchy equivalent to a second government. Coordinating these would be handled by a central Ministry of Local Government; a Turkish minister would serve as an additional safeguard for the interests of the Turkish community.

Greek proposal

The Greek delegation proposes that the local administration of Cyprus be organized primarily along geographical rather than communal lines.

Turkish villages and municipalities would continue electing their own councils, but no island-wide administrative hierarchy based upon ethnic affiliation would be created.

Final supervisory authority would be retained by the Interior Ministry and the district administrators who would oversee local government throughout the Republic.

The central question remained whether or not the Turkish community could preserve its own administrative organization without possessing a separate territory. Our delegation had relinquished the latter, but was not yet prepared to abandon the former.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 17, 1974, Police and internal security
body:
The negotiations concerning local government had naturally led the delegations towards another question, which the Turkish community considered to be perhaps even more important than the administration of its villages: who would be responsible for maintaining law and order?

The events of December 1963 and the years which followed had left the Turkish Cypriots with little faith in the security institutions of the Republic. Our delegation contended that the existence of a single national police force was not necessarily undesirable, provided that the Turkish community had sufficient influence over the officers who would be responsible for maintaining security in its settlements.

The Greeks, however, contended that granting either community authority over the police would undermine the sovereignty of the central government. There could not be two independent security structures operating within the same republic, especially after the intercommunal fighting which had brought the country to its present situation.

A common police force was therefore acceptable to both sides in principle. The disagreement concerned its composition, command and the authority which Turkish local administrations would possess over its activities.

Turkish proposal

A single Cyprus Police would continue to exist under the Constitution, preserving the formal unity of the Republic's law-enforcement institutions.

However, police units operating in Turkish villages and municipalities would be composed predominantly of Turkish personnel, while the Turkish local authorities would possess considerable influence over their everyday duties, responsibilities and operational priorities.

The Constitution would guarantee that at least 20% of all police personnel were Turkish Cypriots. Furthermore, the Deputy Commander of the Cyprus Police would be a Turkish Cypriot, ensuring that the community possessed representation within the highest levels of the police command.

Compromise

Cyprus would retain a unified police and gendarmerie, with Turkish Cypriots comprising 20% of its personnel.

In areas inhabited by both communities, mixed police units would be employed wherever practically possible. Areas inhabited overwhelmingly by Turkish Cypriots would instead be served by Turkish personnel.

Appointments and promotions would be supervised by an independent commission, rather than being left entirely to the discretion of the central government. The Chief and Deputy Chief would belong to different communities.

Local administrations would also be permitted to employ civilian inspectors, although the police and gendarmerie themselves would remain unified institutions.

Greek proposal

The Cyprus Police would remain an entirely centralized institution under the authority of the Republic.

The government would seek to maintain approximately 20% Turkish representation in the police, but neither community would possess separate institutional authority over the force.

Turkish-speaking officers could be assigned to Turkish settlements when necessary, but this would remain an administrative practice rather than a constitutional right or a separate communal police power.

For our delegation, the distinction was a serious one. A promise to employ Turkish officers could always be altered by a future government. A constitutional guarantee, however, would be considerably more difficult to disregard.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 18, 1974, Courts and constitutional disputes
body:
Having discussed matters concerning political representation, local government and internal security, the delegations turned their attention to the judiciary.

It was an issue which might seem less urgent than the deployment of soldiers or the command of the police, but whose implications for the future of the Turkish community could be equally important. After all, even the most carefully drawn constitutional safeguards would be of little value if the courts which had responsibility for interpreting them could be controlled by the Greek majority.

The original Constitution of 1960 had sought to solve this problem with a strange judicial arrangement designed to preserve the independence of the courts from either community. Yet the constitutional disputes which had followed independence had shown how difficult such an arrangement was to maintain.

Our delegation was now ready to accept a unified judiciary, but insisted that Turkish representation within the higher courts had to be guaranteed. The Greek representatives preferred a judiciary whose appointments and organization would gradually cease to be dictated by the ethnic affiliation of its judges.

Turkish proposal

Cyprus would retain a single judiciary, with a Supreme Court composed of six Greek Cypriot and three Turkish Cypriot judges.

The Turkish Vice-President would have a decisive role in the nomination of Turkish judges, preventing the Greek-controlled institutions of the central government from appointing the representatives of the Turkish community without its consent.

Whenever a case concerned the constitutional rights of the Turkish Cypriots, it would have to be heard by a judicial panel which included at least one Turkish judge.

Specialized courts dealing with local-government disputes could also be established, providing an additional means of resolving disagreements between communal administrations and the central government.

Compromise

The existing constitutional and supreme courts would be merged into a single higher court consisting of six Greek Cypriot and three Turkish Cypriot judges.

Turkish members of the court would be formally appointed by the President, but from candidates preferred by the Turkish Vice-President.

Ordinary courts would remain part of a unified judicial system. However, parties appearing before them would have the right to request a judge speaking their own language or belonging to their own community.

Disputes concerning local government would be assigned to specialist judges operating within the independent judiciary, rather than to separate communal courts.

Greek proposal

The Greek delegation proposes the establishment of a fully unified judiciary, with judicial appointments made through a common Judicial Council.

The existing ethnic quotas would gradually be abolished, allowing judges to be appointed without permanently reserving particular positions for either community.

Turkish constitutional rights would instead be protected by a written catalogue of rights and the ordinary powers of judicial review exercised by the courts.

No separate Turkish courts or judicial veto powers would be established.

The disagreement concerned whether the Turkish community should have an institutional role in the administration of justice, or whether its security could be entrusted to the constitutional independence of the judiciary.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 19, 1974, International guarantees
body:
The constitutional negotiations were now reaching one of their most delicate issues, and perhaps the one on which Turkey had the strongest position: the international guarantees for Cyprus’s independence and the security of its inhabitants.

Since the Republic’s establishment, Turkey, Greece, and Britain had been obliged to protect Cyprus’s independence and territorial integrity under the Treaty of Guarantee. However, the Greek coup and Paphos’s events showed that these measures were insufficient to prevent attempts to change the constitutional order. On the other hand, our intervention in Cyprus demonstrated the different guarantors’ willingness to protect the status quo in the country.

In particular, for our delegates, the events of the last month confirmed the necessity of Turkey’s right to intervene if the Turkish Cypriots are at risk. At the same time, the Greek delegation insisted that unilateral interventions of any of the guarantors would leave Cyprus vulnerable to another foreign takeover.

Britain was also dissatisfied with the guarantee system, as it tried to balance its commitments to Cyprus, Turkey, and Greece throughout the complicated events.

Therefore, it was now necessary to decide on the guarantees to be provided to Cyprus in the future.

Options for Agreement

Turkey’s proposal

The original 1960 treaty would be modified slightly to maintain the status quo of three guarantors but include a permanent UN supervision mechanism for Cyprus’s security.

The right of unilateral intervention of any of the guarantors would be retained, as it was vital to ensure that the guarantor states could respond promptly and effectively to violations of the constitutional order in Cyprus. However, a dispute resolution mechanism was required to prevent disagreements between guarantor states from undermining international commitments or delaying responses to crises.

Compromise proposal

The 1960 Treaty of Guarantee would be maintained, but its implementation would be overseen by a formal joint constitutional commission, in which violations of the order would be discussed, and solutions would be proposed. First, the dispute between Turkey and Greece would need to be resolved through direct consultations, and then the UN would be tasked with examining the facts of alleged treaty violations. In turn, simultaneous interventions by Turkey, Greece, and Britain, as guarantors, would be necessary to restore order in Cyprus.

However, the right of unilateral intervention by any of the guarantors would be preserved, but only in two cases: another coup attempt to establish Enosis or an imminent attack on one of the communities. The UN would be involved in all stages of verification and fact-finding before any interventions took place.

Greek proposal

According to the Greek delegation, the right of unilateral intervention by any of the guarantor states should be eliminated. Turkey, Greece, and Britain would have political guarantees of Cyprus’s independence and territorial integrity provided through international law and the UN Security Council. However, none of the three states could resort to military intervention in Cyprus unilaterally.

For Turkey, this solution was unacceptable, as it would deprive us of the right to protect the Turkish Cypriot community as we saw fit. Could Greece and Britain guarantee that their military forces would not intervene in Cyprus’s affairs unilaterally in the future? Would the international community respond to another coup in Cyprus with enough speed and force to restore the status quo? These were the questions our delegation wanted to ask the Greek and British delegates.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 20, 1974, The prohibition of Enosis and continuity of the state
body:
The constitutional negotiations finally focused on the crucial issue that has been at the heart of the Cyprus dispute: whether Cyprus would remain independent or whether one of its communities would turn to unification with another country.

For Turkey, Cyprus’s independence, which was ensured when the Republic was established in 1960, was non-negotiable. It was in Greece’s interest that the independence of Cyprus not be jeopardized, as the Turkish Cypriots would not agree to being annexed by Greece.

The July 15 coup, which deposed Makarios and was carried out with the support of the Greek military junta, provided another example of how Enosis proponents threatened to destroy Cyprus’s independence. At the same time, the Greek delegation wanted to ensure that the new constitution would not allow the permanent division of Cyprus or its unitary independence as a Turkish state.

Both delegations, therefore, agreed that Cyprus’s independence as a whole or in part had to be preserved. They differed in their views on whether this guarantee should be absolute or subject to specified exceptions.

Turkish proposal

The new constitution will include a general and irrevocable ban on joining Cyprus, either in whole or in part, to another state.

A constitutional prohibition shall apply to Enosis, partition, or secession, without any possibility of derogation.

Turkey and Greece will issue a joint declaration banning Enosis and partition and obliging both countries to respect Cyprus’s independence.

Compromise

Cyprus will be guaranteed to remain an independent, sovereign, and indivisible republic with a bicommunal administration.

Enosis, partition, and secession are prohibited by the constitution, with reinforced parliamentary majorities required for any amendment that would derogate from Cyprus’s independence.

Any changes to the constitution are subject to a reinforced parliamentary majority and the agreement of both parliaments, with a view to preventing either of them from forcing a decision through on its own.

Further Greek proposal

Our delegation considers that it cannot accept further concessions on the prohibition of Enosis. Turkey has abandoned its efforts to secure geographical autonomy and agreed to preserve Cyprus as a republic; undermining the prohibition against joining another country or being annexed by it, however, would damage the island’s independence, which both sides have agreed to protect. There can therefore be no agreement in principle on the possibility of Enosis or partition.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 21, 1974, The position of Turkish and Greek troops
body:
The negotiations on the future of Cyprus were now reaching their final test, and one that would decide whether the entire settlement would succeed or collapse: that of the Turkish army's withdrawal and the future of the military forces on the island.

For the Greeks, the continued presence of Turkish soldiers was an unacceptable consequence of the intervention, and the restoration of a united constitution would have to be accompanied by their withdrawal. Our delegation, however, maintained that ordering the army to leave before the new institutions had been properly established would leave the Turkish Cypriots exposed to the same dangers which had brought us to Cyprus in the first place.

There was also the question of the Greek officers serving in the National Guard, the continued existence of Turkish and Greek Cypriot paramilitary organizations, and the military contingents which Turkey and Greece had been permitted to station on the island under the agreements of 1960.

Our government was prepared to withdraw the additional forces sent to Cyprus, but the timing of their departure was a matter of some disagreement.

Turkish proposal

The Turkish forces which had landed on July 20 would not be withdrawn immediately following a constitutional settlement.

Their withdrawal would instead be made after the new Constitution had been implemented, the Turkish local police organizations had been established, and the necessary reforms of the National Guard had been completed with the new security guarantees ratified.

Once these conditions had been fulfilled, the Turkish and Greek military presence would eventually be reduced to the contingents permitted under the agreement of 1960: 650 Turkish and 950 Greek soldiers.

The Turkish Resistance Organization, or TMT, and the Greek Cypriot paramilitary organizations would be dismantled simultaneously, preventing either community from being left unprotected while the other retained its military formations.

Compromise

The Turkish army would initially remain within the territory they had controlled along the ceasefire line, but would not be able to expand this position any further.

Under the supervision of the United Nations, the Turkish landing force would be reduced in parallel with the withdrawal of Greek officers and other unauthorized personnel.

Heavy weapons would also be removed from the National Guard and TMT as part of the process of reducing the military capabilities of the two communities.

As the new constitutional institutions began to function, the Turkish and Greek forces would gradually be reduced to their respective treaty contingents of 650 and 950 soldiers, a process which would take three to six months to complete.

The arrangement would remain subject to further review once the security situation had stabilized.

Greek proposal

All Turkish soldiers who had landed on Cyprus on July 20 would be required to withdraw according to a short timetable following a settlement.

Greece would simultaneously withdraw the officers involved in the coup and all other Greek military personnel not permitted under the original treaties.

TMT would be dissolved, while the National Guard would be restored to the control of the legitimate Cypriot government.

In the long term, the Greek delegation also wishes to examine the complete withdrawal of even the treaty-authorized Turkish and Greek contingents, transferring responsibility for the island's security to United Nations forces and international guarantees.

Our delegation was now being asked to decide how much protection the Turkish Cypriots could reasonably expect from their new constitutional rights, and at what point the army which had secured their safety could finally return home.

The future of the entire agreement depended upon the answer.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
title: August 21, 1974, The constitutional treaty
body:
After more than eight days of hard bargaining, the delegations in Geneva finally arrived at an agreement on the constitutional future of Cyprus. Thus, the Turkish government, which had surprisingly renounced further claims of territorial autonomy, presented the Republic with an alternative solution to the one provided by the 1960 Constitution.

The agreement made provision for a settlement of powers between the central government and the communities, the political status of Turkish Cypriots, their administration, police, and judiciary, as well as the guarantees for the independence of Cyprus, the illegality of Enosis, and the withdrawal of Turkish and Greek troops. Moreover, the agreement stipulated the partition of Cyprus and prohibited both Enosis and partition in the future.

It goes without saying that not everything in the agreement was to our liking. Many concessions had to be made during the course of the negotiations and the Turkish Cypriots would hardly consider themselves to be as autonomous as they should be. In addition, the settlement was to be significantly different from the one proposed by Turkey at the beginning of the conflict.

However, at least Cyprus would remain an independent republic under the sovereignty of two communities. Turkish Cypriots would not receive the geographical autonomy that Denktaş had requested, but their future political prospects would depend on the agreements reached in Geneva.

It was now up to Prime Minister Ecevit to decide whether to accept or reject the agreement. The decision to sign the treaty would enable him to end the Cyprus crisis, which had been dragging on for so long, and allow Turkey to withdraw its troops in accordance with the terms of the agreement. On the other hand, he would have to admit that Turkey would not be able to complete the task of implementing the territorial integrity of the Republic as promised by his country’s army.

On the other hand, rejecting the agreement and declaring a military operation would provide the opposite result. The Cyprus crisis would continue, as the negotiations would enter a new round, while the Turkish army would attack Cyprus to achieve the purpose that the diplomats failed to attain.

Thus, after weeks of hesitation between two options, the future of Cyprus now depended on one decision – whether to accept the new terms of the agreement and end the crisis or to continue believing in the military operations carried out by the Turkish army.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
note: Constitutional settlement outcome, strongest Turkish protections
body:
After eight days of negotiations, the new constitutional agreement has finally been signed. The Cyprus crisis ended without another military operation. The Republic would remain united, but its Constitution would be significantly different from the one which had governed the island since 1960.

And what an agreement our delegation has secured!

Although we had given up on our claim for a separate Turkish region, Turan Güneş and his delegation managed to obtain practically all the constitutional guarantees Turkey subsequently presented to the conference. The Turkish community would have its own political representation, considerable autonomy over its local affairs, guaranteed participation in the police and judiciary, and protection against unilateral changes to its constitutional status.

The Treaty of Guarantee would continue to be in force, giving Turkey the right to intervene as a last resort, but the prohibition of Enosis would now be permanent. Even the withdrawal of our army would be contingent upon the implementation of the new institutions and security arrangements.

For Denktaş, who has been demanding effective protection for his community for so many years, it was a significant achievement. Although the Turkish Cypriots would continue to be scattered throughout the island rather than confined to a single territory, they would now have constitutional guarantees which the Greek majority could not simply repeal at will.

The news of the agreement was received with satisfaction in Ankara. Prime Minister Ecevit has shown that the strength gained by the military intervention could be used to secure a diplomatic settlement without the army having to advance any further. Our government has achieved what many thought impossible only a few days ago, and public confidence in its ability to manage the Cyprus crisis has grown.

The success was also reflected in the popularity of CHP, whose support grew by approximately three percentage points in the opinion polls.

For the first time since the troubles of 1963, it seems that there may be some hope that the Turkish Cypriots can live in peace within a united Cyprus, not as a community dependent on the goodwill of the majority, but as a people whose rights are protected by the very essence of the Republic.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
body:
The constitutional treaty was finally signed, putting an end to the negotiations which had occupied the delegations during the preceding eight days. Cyprus would continue to exist as a unitary and independent republic, governed by a modified version of the constituent order established in 1960.

There was understandable relief in Ankara, although the agreement was by no means the success our government had initially hoped to achieve.

We had entered the crisis demanding that the Turkish Cypriots no longer be dependent upon the establishments of a state whose constitutional order had collapsed more than a decade previously. However, after the intervention, the Geneva Conferences and following all the political difficulties which then ensued, we had abandoned our demand for geographical autonomy and accepted a settlement which was based upon a variety of compromises.

Nevertheless, it would be unfair to describe the negotiations as a complete failure. The Turkish community had managed to secure a series of new constitutional safeguards, representation in the institutions of the Republic and arrangements intended to prevent the recurrence of the disputes which had resulted in the island's present situation. The agreement was certainly not everything Denktaş had demanded, but neither was it merely a restoration of the old Constitution.

For Ecevit, the most important achievement was perhaps that the crisis had finally ended without yet another offensive. Turkish soldiers would be able to return home under the terms of the settlement, while the two Cypriot communities would once again have an opportunity to establish a functioning republic.

The agreement was received with cautious approval by much of the Turkish public and the CHP enjoyed an increase of approximately three percentage points in the opinion polls. However, there were also those who questioned whether the government had relinquished too much after the sacrifices already rendered by our armed forces.

Only time would decide if the constitutional guarantees which had been negotiated at Geneva would prove sufficient.

We had avoided another war and obtained a new political arrangement for Cyprus. Now it was the responsibility of both communities, and the three guarantor powers, to ensure that the same constitutional disputes would not lead the island into another crisis.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
body:
The constitutional agreement had finally been signed and, with it, the Cyprus crisis came to an end. The Republic would remain united (its territorial integrity intact) and the amended constitution would replace the one that had governed Cyprus since independence.

But there was little rejoicing among the members of our delegation as negotiations wound down.

What began as a Turkish military intervention designed to secure the future of Turkish Cypriots had resulted in an agreement that fell far short of our original aims. Geographical autonomy was abandoned, and many of our delegation's proposed constitutional reforms were either watered down or given up entirely.

While the agreement did offer some protection for Denktaş and the Turkish community from a return to the situation that had existed before July 20th, much of their future security would again depend on the will of the Greek majority to respect the institutions of the Republic and the ability of the international guarantors to enforce the settlement in case of another crisis.

In Ankara, the government tried to put the best face on things by pointing out that Turkey had prevented a wider war and obtained a peaceful constitutional settlement for Cyprus. The Turkish Cypriots were no longer threatened with immediate military action, and the country had avoided catastrophic diplomatic and economic fallout that another offensive might have caused.

There was some truth in that argument, but it did little to disguise the disappointment felt by those who believed that Turkey had failed to take advantage of the military and diplomatic advantage it had acquired.

The conclusion of the crisis still managed to provide Ecevit and CHP with a shot in the arm, with the pro-Cyprus party gaining three percentage points in the opinion polls. While the end of hostilities was welcomed, those concessions made at Geneva were already being heavily criticized.

Turkey may have won peace, but at the expense of giving up much of what it had originally wanted.

Whether or not this settlement would last, or simply put off the Cyprus question for another generation, was something neither the diplomats in Geneva nor the politicians in Ankara could know.

part: PART VIII, REVISED UNITED CYPRUS CONSTITUTION: EIGHT DEBATES AND OUTCOMES
note: Abandon constitutional talks and authorize Atilla II
title: Ayşe Tatile Çıksın
body:
The Turkish government had finally decided that there was nothing to be gained from continuing the constitutional negotiations at Geneva. Our delegation had poured hours into finding an arrangement that would allow the Turkish Cypriot community to live securely within a united republic, but Ankara had concluded that such an agreement would not provide the territorial security desired.

It had not been an easy decision. Turkey had already shown tremendous flexibility by giving up on the demand for geographical autonomy and accepting the prospect of new constitutional discussions. Yet we were clearly unwilling to leave the security of the Turkish community to another set of constitutional promises, which had proved so disastrous.

For Ecevit, the alternative had been obvious from the start of the Geneva talks. The General Staff had continued to prepare its forces during the ceasefire, and the reinforcements sent to the island had vastly improved the Turkish military position. The army was no longer restricted to the small bridgehead in place at the beginning of the intervention, or suffering from the shortages and confusion of the first landings.

And so, with the decision finally made in Ankara, the waiting message for the commanders was delivered.

"Ayşe Tatile Çıksın."

There would be no further negotiations.

The orders were passed to the military headquarters, and the preparations which had kept the General Staff occupied for the past few weeks finally began. Soldiers were ordered into their armoured vehicles, artillery positions were readied for the offensive and the Turkish Air Force was directed to support the advance. The target was the Şahin Line, the broad territorial position that would extend Turkish control across the northern part of Cyprus.

At Geneva, the decision brought the negotiations to a premature end. Whatever constitutional arrangements had been discussed would now be left without their final settlement, as our delegation announced that Turkey was no longer willing to continue the conference. The Greek and British representatives protested at the decision, warning that another military operation would bring serious international consequences.

But the orders had already been given.

With Turkish aircraft once again sweeping over Cyprus and armoured formations beginning their advance from the territory secured during Atilla I, the Second Cyprus Peace Operation had begun.

The future of the island would now be decided, at least for the time being, not by the diplomats around the conference table, but by the soldiers fighting across its battlefields.
